Very fun game. I don't have anything else to say. 5 stars.

Random part usages and interactions aren't clear; game forces you to choose a pilot class and, if you mess up and choose fully autonomous, your ship does nothing (even loaded up with sensors) and you effectively have to start the game again from scratch.. fully autonomous doesn't mean intermittent triggers of random parts will result in accomplishing any given mission, so it's confusing to have as an option: I fail to see how even an "expert" could setup a ship to do 'anything at all' autonomously, if the game's not intuitive enough to make it obvious how to get an autonomous drone to fire a single thruster.

Further, the game warns you that you have too many parts attached to the same part which may cause instability; yet everything seems to attach to the main base core anyway- so it's also confusing as to what you're supposed to do with what's provided; as everything I built seems functional, yet I get reminded through icons that my build isn't ideal. 

They should give you a tutorial overview of a build which employs all part types and demonstrates how each part interacts, instead of skimming over the shallow basics- then hinting at more tutorial interactions.

Since it's been about 6 months, it's unlikely this game will get any more attention from the studio, which is probably why they're dropping it to $5; yet I'm less interested in trying to figure out what all the random parts are for, when the game fails to make it clear as to their use-cases and, apparently, it's expected that players will have to watch tutorial vids on youtube just to figure out things that aren't worth figuring out.

Корабль игрока собирается из разных функциональных блоков. Сам процесс строительства к сожалению почти ничего от игрока не требует. Набор блоков интересный, но единственная задача на всю игру, это удержание структуры стабильной - Если слишком много блоков будут висеть на одном блоке, или блоки будут слишком далеко друг от друга, они будут шататься и легко ломаться. В остальном вообще плевать, что, как и куда ставить: Пушки спокойно стреляют в любую сторону сквозь корабль игрока; Энергетические батареи и топливные баки могут располагаться вообще где угодно, относительно блоков потребителей; Сборщики ресурсов и грузовые отсеки могут располагаться вообще где угодно относительно друг друга. Что бы вы не построили, оно все равно будет работать. Развиваться и придумывать что то интересное здесь почти не в чем. Исключение все таки есть, это блоки автоматизации, всякие датчики, механизмы и так далее. Но это фича чисто для творческого режима и каких мелких аркадных режимов. В основной компании реализовать что то такое очень тяжело да и не нужно, о чем прямым текстом говорит обучение игры.

К слову об одиночной компании. Посредственность основного игрового режима это болезнь многих игр конструкторов, но здесь компания реализована особенно ужасно. В ходе компании игрок зачищает планеты, выполняя на них различные активности. Основной костяк активностей представляет из себя такую невероятную деятельность, как: Афк долбежка жирных ассетов; Таскание мусора, со сломанной физикой/коллизией и дополнительными багами; И пылесосинг луж ресурсов по зажатию одной кнопки. За зачистку планет даются различные награды, в частности блоки для строительства. Но блоков дается невероятно мало, а структурных, которые помогут стабилизировать и увеличить постройку, ещё меньше. Строить и глобально менять свой корабль просто не из чего. Блоки также можно покупать в магазинах, вот только вся валюта на покупку блоков уходит на покупку жизней для своей "Базы".

"Базой" я назвал декоративный корабль, на котором как бы и происходит перемещение между планетами. У игрока есть шкала угрозы. Шкала заполняется от перелетов между планетами и системами, от самого спуска на планету, и в рандомных ивентах. Причем в лишний раз заполнить её очень просто. Например зачастую игроку приходится спуститься на планету, увидеть и понять, что там вообще за хрень от него требуют и какие опасности там есть, помереть, в лучшем случае только один раз, стакнув себе при этом процент угрозы, а потом спуститься уже готовым. Вернуться в магазин, в котором вы уже были, на практике самоубийство, потому что процент угрозы от такого полета туда сюда стакается очень быстро. При заполнении этой шкалы примерно до 90% случается событие, при котором база игрока теряет единицу прочности. Если база будет уничтожена, игра нах_й снесет вам сохранение компании, убив и так очень медленный и унылый прогресс, и предлагая импортировать сохраненные чертежи кораблей в креатив. То есть игра штрафует вас за каждое движение по карте; Убивает вас по незнанию и штрафует за это; Штрафует рандомными ивентами; Заставляет вас вкладываться не в блоки для строительства, а жизни; А потом сносит вам сохранение. After buying and playing for about 1.5 hours I think the trailer is deceptive in setting expectations for the game which is what motivated the review. 

The control scheme is more like an experimental robotics student project than a game and does not perform the way the trailer suggests. You don't have intentional (ie vectoring) control over your ship's movement. Think the old school game asteroid's movement scheme where you only had rotation + forward vectoring. It's like that, but you have to hit a different key for each thruster you add (or groups) and imbalances are frequent causing your ship to move erratically or spin uncontrollably. You get a warning in the game about this, but it feels like the dev is telling me "that would be hard to design better so I'll just tell you not to do it instead". It seems to me they avoided showing longer clips of navigation purposefully. 

I don't mind difficulty when it's an interesting puzzle. But this is just difficult to manage, eating up your time and frustration without purpose. Nobody would design a vehicle propulsion interface to work like this. Seems like a pet project idea that wasn't user tested enough. 

There are other usability irritants in the UI building ships (repetitive mouse strokes, doesn't remember common configurations, etc...) that make the user experience inconvenient. Needs user research feedback and changes to core movement system to reduce friction building and controlling ships. In it's current state it's not worth the level of fighting with the application to find enjoyment.

TLDR: The game looked awesome in the store but when playing it, it was immediately clear that the game is very cheap, quality-wise.


I like designing, driving and destroying ships/contraptions. I like physics and destructible terrain. I'm interested in "exploring a procedural universe".
This game seemed made for me, but all of these features ended up being pretty superficial. It felt like I was playtesting a prototype that would be improved later, not a fully-released game.


-- Mining --
For a game about digging and collecting resources, it feels really bad to do either. It lacks feedback/complexity/balance.
You can damage the terrain with weapons or dig ores with this nearly-imperceptible vacuum turret. In both cases, a chunk of whatever you are targeting simply poofs out of existence, with the ores cosmetically flying towards your ship. When your storage is full, the ore vacuum turret still turns on but magically stops affecting the ore.
There is just no satisfying two-step "turn big rock into small rock then gather those" feel - you turn big rock into nothing, or an invisible stored item.
As a contextual example: imagine if in Minecraft instead of resources breaking into item drops you mined them directly into your inventory, and when your inventory is full you can still swing your pickaxe at blocks but it simply does nothing.

Also, despite the physics-based flying, I don't think the weight of the ore you hold affects the handling. At the very least, after fitting an asteroid 10 times the size of my entire ship into a small box inside it, I did not notice any difference when flying away.


-- Ship design --
The ship design system is very simple and gives you too much freedom. The only thing that really matters is if things are connected (and apparently being connected becomes optional later?) and if enemy damage won't immediately hit something important.
All parts effectively cost the same, as the build cost scales only by how many parts you equip. That makes it so two tiny featureless armor cubes cost twice as much as a massive rocket thruster.
You can point thrusters directly into each other or other parts with no consequence. Similarly, my character started with flamethrowers so I set them up in the front and made sure to design the ship light and maneuverable with strong forward thrust to quickly approach a target then keep it in front of me... only to find out I was able to just aim them directly backwards, right through my entire ship with no consequence.


-- Physics --
In this game you build ships by freely attaching parts to a static "center core", using some dynamic-length connector, and as you run out of space in the center you can attach new parts to the other parts and so on.
Despite the entire building part of the game being done with these connections, it seems their physics are very buggy, so much so that the building tutorial itself goes out of its way to warn you about it.
The warning made me want to test this so I added 4 symmetric double-jointed straight arms at max connection length (which is very short, mind you) to the core and sure enough, as soon as I entered the test drive it immediately started a cascading physics death-wobble. When something this simple and of static design, with no thrusters or gravity to even affect it in the first place breaks like this, it makes me wonder how much "bug fixing" patchwork I'd need to do in a bigger and more complex design.
Look, I've played enough Garry's Mod to get PTSD from these things, just imagining building a whole thing to see it fail because the engine decides it can't handle the physics between connected parts. It's not something I'm keen to experience more of.


-- Conclusion --
It is actually kind of interesting how quickly and strongly this game put me off, maybe a stacking effect as every single new feature I experienced was so different from what I was expecting (or hoping?).
I don't recall any other game giving me such a strong "I need to stop playing and refund this right now" feeling before and this is my first time feeling the need to review a game I've refunded.

I've done two full playthroughs of this game at least, one on the programmer archetype and one without.  The programmer archetype radically changes the game and provides a niche experience where you quite literally program the drones to complete objectives, without any direct inputs during missions.  If you've ever played the old PS1 game Carnage Heart, this game scratches the same sort of niche.  The tradeoff for relinquishing user inputs is that you basically get free reign to go full sandbox mode on your drones in the campaign, with all available blocks and no build restrictions.  So if the mission objective is simple like destroy the target, you could make a drone that infinitely replicates large drilling missiles that fire down into the planet towards the objective, and just turn the whole planet into swiss cheese.  Most of the other missions involve retrieving something and bringing it back to the main cargo bay, though there's a few solutions you can program in order to do this properly without direct inputs (usually either by combing across the top of the planet horizontally, or drilling through it to grab the object and then return to the cargo thignie)

There's a decent number of curveballs and challenges the game presents but it's sadly just a little too short for my liking, they also aren't updating this further.  They really don't make enough of this type of game, very unique sort of experience,  I think the game's passable without the programmer archetype as a basic ship builder but it really shines if you're willing to restrict yourself to the logic blocks

Overall the game is not bad, but some things prove impossible to achieve. In this review I will say what makes me not able to reccomend it. I will not talk about the positive aspects of the game.
Small drones work very well, and they are fun to make, control or automate. However when designing autonomous drones for more complex tasks, a bigger drone is usually needed. Sadly, making big drones is very difficult and wonky.
Building in this game works by allowing you to connect one part to another, by using a semi rigid connection. This causes 2 major issues.
First you cannot choose the connections freely. One is created when placing a new part - it is formed between an already existing part and the one you are trying to place. Additional connections are created when repeating this process with an another new part. This makes it impossible to create closed loops and other complex (stable) geometry. For example if you create a ring from basic blocks, you cannot connect the ends together - if you select the last block of the ring, and try to attach it to the beginning, it disconnects from the end. Technically this would have been fine is the connections were completely rigid - this brings us to the second major problem.
The connections are effectively springs with varying strength and stability. The shorter the connection, the more stable it is (in theory). The game also takes into account the weight of the part at which the connection originates (the one you select when placing a new part), when deciding the stability. The effects of these attributes are rarely noticable in small drones. The worst that can happen is a thruster sliding a bit when active. Returning to my previous major issue, this combined with not being able to link together parts, the spring-like quality makes all shapes wobbly and "squishy" under force. Even if you are not making complex shapes, a simple collision can make an element change its place, which in turn could colide or twist another.
Even if you avoid long connections, it remains wobbly. A simple "bridge" made of standard 2x1 pieces easily bends if you put a thruster onto it.
You could technically try to learn the softbody nature of drones in this game, which would allow you to build more easily, but I think that it is too gimmicky and unpredictable to consider buying this game for the building aspect (which is the main selling point).

This is a spaceship construction game where you design space drones and then send them on missions to planetary surfaces where you pilot the drone to do things like destroy space monster eggs or retrieve an item.

THE GOOD:
- There are a decent variety of parts to experiment with.
- There is decent variety in the mission types, which requires you to do some problem solving to design the right types of drones.
- You can come up with some clever designs. I was particularly proud of my lifter drone that had automation allowing it to stay upright. Instead of thrusting forward like a plane, it could move left, right, up, or down, making it easy to approach and grab objects on the ground.
- You can test out your drone designs before sending them out into the field.

THE BAD:
- The heart and soul of this game is the drone construction, and it's deeply flawed. Each drone part can only connect to one other part, leading to strange and unstable drones where every part must connect to the center.
- The missions generally feel really long, and they're often not particularly interesting.
- There are often strange hiccups, like tiny pieces of land your drone gets stuck on.
- Mining for minerals feels repetitive pretty quickly.
- I tried really hard to like this game, but it's not very fun. There is too much frustration in the drone design and not enough fun in the missions.

THE UGLY:
- Drones will get shaky and vibrate due to a game engine glitch and you can't fix this by adding triangular braces.
- Certain objects were sliding up the magnet (when I was capturing them) and causing my drone to go haywire. It was really weird.

I'd been watching Nimbatus for quite some time, waiting for it to exit Early Access. I'm always eager to play this type of game, like Reassembly. I'm always disappointed. This time I was certain events would reconfigure themselves. The massive constructions in the videos on the Steam store page blasted away my doubts. In Nimbatus the player travels from planet to planet, pursued by The Corp. The story is irrelevant. The player chooses planets to explore. Or skips over them to move onto new galaxies. With the Corp in pursuit the player can't waste time. On each planet the player has an objective which rewards them with new starship pieces. In addition to the objective, planets contain two minerals, a red one and a gold one. Unfortunately, completing the objective, which involves killing enemy forces, and collecting the necessary resources, necessitates two different styles of ships.

The player needs one ship with lasers, shotguns, and rocket launchers, and another with drills, a resource collector, and a tank. In the beginning the player is limited to a small ship, while purchasable upgrades eventually allow for a larger ship. These were issues, but not problems. The problem is that every planet is nearly the same. They all contain a weak ground force (a few turrets, a handful of weak fighter ships,) and some resources to mine. Across a dozen planets I experienced zero cool space battles between larger ships or fleets. Maybe those would eventually arrive, but after three and a half hours squashing small alien bees or pathetic anti-aircraft guns you'd jump out the airlock too.
